summary.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest in the Solar System after Jupiter, a gas giant.
Its bright rings are mainly ice particles, and at least 293 moons orbit it, including Titan, the only moon with a substantial atmosphere.
Though almost as big as Jupiter, it has less than a third of its mass, and it is the only planet less dense than water.

items.prompt: Saturn is far more massive than Earth, yet much less dense. How can both be true?

options.label: Its core is hollow
It is huge in volume and made mostly of light hydrogen and helium
It is mostly frozen water with little rock
Its rings carry away most of its mass

items.explain: It has an average radius about 9 times Earth's and is mostly hydrogen and helium, so its density is an eighth of Earth's.

items.prompt: Saturn looks pale yellow. What gives it that hue?

options.label: Sulfur dust from its volcanoes
Sulfuric acid clouds across the planet
Ammonia crystals in its upper atmosphere
Methane absorbing red light

items.explain: Saturn has a pale yellow hue due to ammonia crystals in its upper atmosphere.

items.prompt: Saturn gives off more energy than it gets from the Sun, and slow squeezing alone may fall short. What extra source is suggested?

options.label: Helium droplets raining through hydrogen
Hydrogen fusion starting up in its core
Tidal flexing from the pull of its moons
Lightning flashing through its bright rings

items.explain: The 'raining out' of helium droplets deep inside could release heat by friction as an alternative or additional mechanism.

items.prompt: Astronomers use three different systems for Saturn's spin rate, not one. Why?

options.label: Its core and rings spin in opposite directions
Its axis flips over time
Instruments disagree about its spin
Its visible features turn at different rates at different latitudes

items.explain: The visible features rotate at different rates depending on latitude, so multiple rotation periods have been assigned.

items.prompt: What sets Titan apart from every other moon in the Solar System?

options.label: It is the only one with a substantial atmosphere
It is the largest moon of all
It is more massive than Mercury
It is the only moon with a name

items.explain: Titan is the only moon in the Solar System that has a substantial atmosphere; it is larger than Mercury but less massive.

items.prompt: Models assumed a small, compact rocky core. What do measurements of Saturn's rings suggest instead?

options.label: No core at all, only gas
A tiny core the size of Earth
A spread-out core reaching about 60% of the way out
A solid iron core 20,000 km wide

items.explain: Ring measurements suggest a much more diffuse core, with a radius about 60% of Saturn's entire radius.

paragraphs.heading: The second giant
paragraphs.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest in the Solar System, after Jupiter. It is a gas giant with an average radius about 9 times Earth's, and it is over 95 times as massive as Earth yet only an eighth as dense. It is close to Jupiter in size, yet it carries under a third of Jupiter's mass. It circles the Sun at 1,434 million km and takes 29.45 years to go around once.

paragraphs.heading: Lighter than water
paragraphs.text: Saturn is made mostly of hydrogen and helium and has no definite surface. It is the only planet in the Solar System less dense than water, by about 30%, with an average density of 0.69 g/cm³. Jupiter has 318 times Earth's mass and Saturn only 95 times, but together the two hold 92% of all the mass in the planets.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the planet
paragraphs.text: Going inward, the temperature, pressure and density all climb steadily, and deep down hydrogen behaves as a metal. The picture is a core of rock and ice, then a thick layer of liquid metallic hydrogen, then liquid hydrogen saturated with helium that slowly turns to gas higher up, topped by a gas layer about 1,000 km deep. The core seems to be diffuse, a gradual blend of rock and ice reaching 60% of the way to the surface. So although Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, most of its mass is not gas. The centre is hot, about 11,700 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Helium rain
paragraphs.text: Saturn gives off 2.5 times more energy than it gets from the Sun. Jupiter makes its heat by slowly squeezing itself under gravity, but that alone may not be enough for Saturn, which has less mass. One idea is that droplets of helium rain down deep inside. As they sink through the lighter hydrogen, friction releases heat, and the outer layers are left short of helium.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetism, colour and wind
paragraphs.text: An electric current in the metallic hydrogen layer is thought to create Saturn's magnetic field. The field is weaker than Earth's, but because Saturn is so much bigger its magnetic moment is 580 times Earth's, and its strength is about a twentieth of Jupiter's. Ammonia crystals high in the atmosphere give the planet its pale yellow colour. The outer atmosphere usually looks bland and low in contrast, though long-lived features can appear, and winds can reach 1,800 km/h.

paragraphs.heading: Rings and moons
paragraphs.text: Saturn's rings are bright and extensive, made mostly of ice particles with smaller amounts of rock and dust. At least 293 moons orbit it, 63 of them officially named, not counting the hundreds of moonlets in the rings. The largest, Titan, is the second biggest moon in the Solar System. It is larger than Mercury, though less massive, and it is the only moon with a substantial atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A name from Rome
paragraphs.text: Its name comes from the Roman god of farming and wealth, the father of the god Jupiter. The Romans also named the seventh day of the week after it: Saturday, or Saturn's Day.
